cells.tense: You can take something in whole and set it down without needing it settled.
cells.ask: Name one thing that has ended, out loud to yourself in plain words. Then spend the next hour starting nothing.
cells.core:
You look at something and take in the whole of it — what it was, what it isn't anymore. That kind of clarity usually arrives late, after the arguing is done. Your honesty gets there early, and you say it without dressing it up.

It isn't the sort that leaves you admiring your own insight. It's plainer. You look at a job, a habit, a version of yourself, and you understand it well enough to put it down. That's the rarer part — knowing something is over and letting it be over. You don't need to force the next thing to appear before you've finished with this one. When the next thing arrives, you'll take that in whole too.

cells.verb: Taking something in whole, with nothing left hidden

cells.tense: You're seeing endings before they've happened, bracing for a moment that hasn't arrived.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've called over and leave it open a week. Don't announce anything. Only move when it shows you.
cells.core:
You're already naming what's finished before it has finished. Somewhere ahead of you is the moment it will be over, and you're living back from it — closing things early, ending them in your head before they end in the world. There's a kind of clear look that settles the future too soon.

The clarity itself is real. Not every end you've called is wrong. The bend is that you want the resolving done before the thing has had its run — to finish the uncertainty rather than the thing. Next time you'd call it over, wait. Hold the open question until it closes itself, then say what you saw.

cells.tense: You've gone quiet on what's finished, and the door stays open a crack.
cells.ask: Write down one next step for after a thing that's already done. One step, plain, on paper you'll see again.
cells.core:
Looking isn't the problem here. Acting on what you see is. You keep the door open a crack, keep it technically undecided, and the undecidedness is doing the work of protecting you. From the outside nothing looks wrong — the situation is just still open, still waiting on better information.

The next step doesn't require the whole thing resolved. Name one concrete thing you'll do once it ends, and write it down where you'll run into it. The shape of the next thing is how the end gets bearable — not the other way around. Nothing about the timing has to be right for you to put one foot where the floor is going.

cells.tense: You're clearing ground around you, and you say the clearing is just how things went.
cells.ask: Say 'I ended that' out loud about something you've been calling the timing, the market, or the way it went.
cells.core:
You're already in the middle of it. Things are ending around you, and by your own account they are just ending — the timing ran out, the fit changed, the season moved. But you're the one who saw which fires to let die, and that choice was yours.

That doesn't mean you chose the loss. Naming what you saw, and acting on it, is you. Look at this week and find one door you quietly stopped knocking on — one you'd say just went quiet. Say out loud that you ended it. Then notice you were there the whole time, and you can be again.

attempts.check: The record does not say the person has already ended anything or grieved a specific loss — only that clarity is operating in the room where endings and clearing live. A reader could say the closing is fine and the seeing is the problem, so the cells locate the bend in the seeing, not in the life. The asks survive a wrong read: each is one visible act about what has been seen, not proof that anything must end. The sentence that serves the writer is the 'already ended it' line — kept out of the Unacknowledged ask so nothing is put in the person's mouth.
